# Week 3 Robot dance studio

> [Download the Word version](W03_dance_Speaker_Notes.docx) · This Markdown copy is generated from the DOCX. Update the DOCX, then run `python scripts/sync_documents.py --write` from the repository root. Print layout, page breaks, headers/footers, and writing-space height remain in Word.

Speaker notes for the seven-slide class presentation. Use the slides as brief prompts and leave time for children to build, operate and explain. This is a robotics session with a small prepared Python recipe.

### Class setup

12 children in grades 5–6 form four teams of three: T1/T2 share Kit A and T3/T4 share Kit B. Four student instructors cover two robot stations and two build tables; a fifth or sixth can float. The adult lead oversees the room and YMCA procedures. Bring four available laptops: two remain connected to robots and two show build references. Printed build cards make the build activity work with two laptops too.

**Learning goal** Each child traces a counted loop and explains which actions repeat and how many times.

**Minimum success** A short routine repeats three times, stays within the test area, and the team accurately predicts the number of movements.

**Prepare** Rehearse W03\_dance.py and the straight cone recipe on both bases. A 90-wheel-degree pivot is not a 90-degree heading change. Pack six matching small cones, four build packs, mounting proxies and two mentor pushers. Mark floor lanes and target zones for the rehearsed travel. Check attachment clearance and swaps; show the hub color guide.

**Materials and files** Print and pack from the matching checklist in 01\_Instructor/Class\_Preparation. Use the team sheet and build card. Keep the original two bases assembled, A left/B right, auxiliary motor unplugged; add C/D only as the lessons require. Hardware rehearsal remains required.

## Slide 1 Robot dance studio

**Timing** 0–5 minutes

**Say** “Today we will use loops for a short robot dance and build an attachment to push a small cone upright into a zone. Everyone will build, operate and explain.”

**Ask before explaining** What made last week’s distance trials a fair comparison?

**Listen for** Change one value and keep the start, floor, robot and speed the same.

## Slide 2 Todays robot challenge

**Timing** 5–10 minutes

**Purpose** Each student traces a counted loop and explains which actions repeat and how many times.

**Do and explain** Compare three copies of two actions with one for loop. Say: “The indented lines belong to the loop.” Trace with a finger three times. Keep the support functions collapsed if the editor allows it.

**Suggested words** “Our useful result today is this: A short routine repeats three times, stays within the test area, and the team accurately predicts the number of movements. A test that misses still gives us information if we record it accurately.”

**Ask** “What did the robot do? What evidence could we record? What must stay the same when we compare the next run?” Let a different student answer each question.

**If the example fails** Only one action repeats: check indentation. SyntaxError after range: check the colon. Dance drifts: reduce travel and recheck the start area; do not chase perfect geometry in this session. Allow one quick reset, then use the prepared stationary or paper explanation. Student testing time should not become a repair demonstration.

**Hub check** Read the light on the correct button: steady green center means powered on with a compatible OS and at least 20% battery; flashing orange center means charge; flashing red center means stop, power off and cool for 15 minutes. White center needs a compatible OS; flashing purple center means updating. Blue is the connection button: flashing means waiting for Bluetooth, steady means connected. A display letter is a program output, not a battery or connection status. See the full SPIKE Hub Color Guide.

## Slide 3 Counted loops and indentation and prediction

**Timing** 10–14 minutes

```python
for beat in range(3):
    await drive(90)
    await turn(90)
await signal("D")
```

**Say** “The line with for tells us how many times to repeat. The indented lines are the actions we repeat. The signal at the left edge happens after the loop.”

**Point** range(3) runs three passes. The colon opens the loop body. Keep drive and turn equally indented; keep the final D outside. Students need not learn the values of beat yet.

**Ask** How many drives? How many turns? Does the final D repeat? Which indentation tells you?

**Expected reasoning** Three drives and three turns. D appears once because it is outside the loop. Moving D inside makes it happen on every pass.

## Slide 4 Our robot and build jobs

**Timing** 14–38 then retests minutes

**Station map** 14–26: T1/T3 use robots and T2/T4 build. 26–38: teams switch stations. 38–44: T1/T3 retest while the other teams finish builds. 44–50: T2/T4 retest. Rotate roles at 18, 22, 30, 34, 40, 42, 46 and 48 minutes. Each team has 18 robot minutes, giving each child about six minutes as driver plus handling, observing and building. Transitions occur within these blocks.

**Jobs** At the robot, the driver edits and starts after “clear.” The navigator reads the step, predicts, positions the stopped robot and payload, fits an approved attachment and checks the lane. The observer watches, measures and records one number, tick or phrase. Rotate all three jobs every four minutes in the first turn and every two minutes in the retest. At the build table, rotate builder, designer/parts manager and tester/reporter on the same timer. Everyone contributes hands-on work.

**Robot steps** 1. Trace the loop with paper arrows. Predict drives, turns and signals. 2. Test three repeats, then two; rotate jobs. 3. Try a short routine with 60–120 wheel degrees and 2–3 repeats. 4. In the final retest, fit the approved cone pusher and use the straight cone recipe below. Predict three drives, three pauses and one D. Each child drives once across the scheduled turns.

**Build** A removable cone pusher. Build a low front bar with two mounting points. Hand-push an upright cone 10 cm, three times, using the mounting proxy. Change height, width or a shallow V to reduce tipping or sideways escape. Keep the cone on the floor; nothing may drag or touch the wheels. Success: cone stays upright with its whole base in the target zone. Keep all attempts and compare one design change.

**Connection to robot** At the stopped robot, a mentor checks clearance and fit. For the cone retest, replace the recipe with three repeats of drive(60) and pause(300), then signal("D") outside the loop. Use await before each command; omit turns. Keep SPEED = 200. Mentor marks a target suited to the rehearsed travel. Stop if the cone falls or escapes; reset only after motion stops. Remove the pusher before a dance run.

**Coaching** Ask for an observation before suggesting a change. Help with one connection or edit, then return control. Typing can be assisted; the child still chooses, predicts and starts the run.

## Slide 5 Build a cone pusher

**Timing** Use as the build-table reference during 14–38 minutes. This is not an extra lecture or time block.

**Mission** Push the cone upright into the zone with its whole base inside. Show the small cone and mounting proxy. The cone stays on the surface; do not lift or carry it.

**Build steps** 1. Make a low front bar with two secure mounting points, using the proxy while the robot is busy. 2. Check floor clearance and the wheel outline; leave robot cables and buttons clear. 3. Hand-push the cone 10 cm toward the zone three times from the same start. 4. Change one feature: contact height, width, bracing or a shallow V with room for the cone. 5. Try three more times and compare successes out of three. Keep the cone, surface, start and travel the same.

**Coach** Ask where the bar touches and what happened before suggesting a solution. If the cone tips, try a lower contact point; if it escapes sideways, try a wider or shallow-V guide. Check whether a brace keeps the shape steady. These are ideas to test, not guaranteed solutions.

**Rotate** Builder connects; designer selects parts and checks fit; tester resets and reports. Rotate every four minutes. Keep every attempt, including tips and escapes.

**Robot handoff** Fit only to a stopped robot after a mentor clearance check. Use the next slide for the straight-loop retest at minutes 38–50. Keep SPEED = 200; no turns. Stop for tipping or escape, then reset only after motion stops. Use the mentor pusher if the team attachment does not fit. Return to reflection at minute 50.

## Slide 6 Evidence from our test

**Timing** 38–50 minutes in two six-minute retests.

**Evidence** At the robot, record repeats and predicted/observed movement counts. At the build table, show three hand trials from the same start: upright in zone, tipped, or escaped. Change one feature and repeat. Use the existing robot trial rows for the cone retest; record failures too.

**Ask** What changed? What stayed the same? What did the real run show? Record a tick, short phrase or number at the robot. The build table tests the model by hand rather than repeating a worksheet.

**Troubleshooting** Only one action repeats: check indentation. SyntaxError after range: check the colon. Dance drifts: reduce travel and recheck the start area; do not chase perfect geometry in this session.

**Support** Provide the complete loop and allow only the number in range to change. Trace with three counters moved one at a time.

**Extension** Define a short async dance\_move function and call it twice, or calibrate a pivot for an approximate corner. Keep this optional and explain the difference between wheel and heading degrees.

**If needed** For the dance: repeat 3 straight moves of 0.25 rotations and a mentor-tested pivot; display D after the loop. For the cone: repeat 3 straight moves of 1/6 rotation and a 0.3-second wait; display D once. No pivot with the cone. Use mentor-tested Word Blocks speeds.

## Slide 7 What we learned and noticed

**Timing** 50–54 minutes for reflection; 54–60 for saving, packing and pickup.

**Ask each child** What did you learn about repeating actions? What did you notice during the robot dance? What would you change in the loop or cone pusher?

**Facilitate** Run two pod conversations in parallel. Give each of the six children about 20–30 seconds for one chosen prompt. Invite a concrete observation from the robot or build. Accept pointing, a demonstration or a short sentence.

**Listen for** Dance: three drives and three turns. Cone: three drives and three pauses. D appears once because it is outside the loop. Moving D inside makes it happen on every pass.

**Close** Save T1–T4 projects, stop and park both robots, remove only approved temporary attachments, store four labeled builds and count parts. Follow YMCA pickup procedures.

**Optional connection** Repeated actions and reusable routines simplify robot programs.
